problem: Legged-robot navigation usually runs a high-level planner and a low-level locomotion controller as separate modules. The planner's cost map comes from vision alone, so it misses glass walls, texture-less or suddenly appearing obstacles, and terrain properties such as slipperiness, softness and roughness. It also ignores payload changes and the walking policy's actual velocity limits.
motivation: Vision is a slow distance sense, while proprioception (joint states, IMU, foot contacts) directly and quickly senses physical interaction with the environment. A planner for a legged robot should know what the locomotion policy can actually do in the current conditions. The paper therefore feeds proprioceptive signals from the walking policy back into the planner online, closing the loop between navigation and locomotion.
key_idea: Freeze an RL velocity-conditioned walking policy and add learned proprioceptive 'safety advisors' (a collision detector and a fall predictor). These insert missed obstacles into a vision-built FMM cost map and cap the commanded speed of a continuous velocity-command planner.
insight: Proprioception catches failure modes vision cannot see, and the benefit grows with difficulty. In Table 1 the collision detector raises SR by 5.70 points with 2 invisible obstacles, 13.35 points with 4 and 14.90 points with 8. In Table 2 the fall predictor adds 7.15 SR under randomized slippery/rough terrain with payload changes, at the cost of longer time to goal (117.65 s vs 105.68 s), because it slows the robot down. Other ablations show that commanding continuous velocities, so the robot can turn and move forward at once, cuts time to goal by about 27% vs a discrete action set (Table 5). An emergent-gait energy-efficient policy lowers energy vs a trot-only policy (Table 3). Legs keep SR at 95.05 on rough terrain where wheels collapse (Table 4).
method: Velocity-conditioned walking policy: an RMA-style base policy (inputs: 30-D proprioception, commanded linear and yaw velocity, previous action, 8-D extrinsics) outputs 12 target joint positions tracked by PD control at 100 Hz. It is trained with PPO in RaiSim on fractal terrains, with a velocity-tracking plus energy-minimization reward that yields emergent gait switching. An adaptation module (75 Hz) estimates the extrinsics from the state-action history for sim-to-real transfer.

Collision Detector Mc: a proprioception-history classifier (linear embedding to 32-D, three 1D-conv layers, MLP, sigmoid). When P(collision) > 0.5 it inserts a 9 cm x 3 cm obstacle patch into the cost map in front of the robot, catching glass walls, humans and texture-less boxes.

Fall Predictor Mf: same architecture; predicts whether the robot will fall within the next 1 s. If P > 0.5 the max velocity limit drops by 0.2 m/s, otherwise it rises by 0.05 m/s. Both advisors are trained self-supervised with BCE on sim rollouts with random invisible obstacles, friction, roughness and payload; the robot version uses a 0.2 s history at 10 Hz.

Visual occupancy mapping: point clouds from a RealSense D435 depth camera are transformed with RealSense T265 tracking-camera pose, height-capped and projected to a 2D occupancy grid (5 Hz). The grid is binarized at 0.5 and dilated to configuration space.

Cost map: FMM geodesic goal distance plus alpha2*max(0, alpha1 - d_sdf), an inverse signed-distance obstacle penalty (alpha1 = 0.3 m, alpha2 = 0.5), giving a smooth map whose steepest descent is a collision-free path.

Velocity command generator (10 Hz): target heading is the negative gradient of the cost map. Angular velocity comes from a PD controller (Kp = 1, Kd = 0.02). Linear velocity comes from a line search for the farthest point along the current heading where cost keeps decreasing (alpha0/T), is exponentially smoothed and clipped to the fall-predictor limit v_max. Angular velocity is clipped to [0.4, 0.8] for in-place turns at low speed.

setting.backbone: MLP walking policy + adaptation module (RMA-style, trained with PPO from scratch) + 1D-conv proprioceptive safety advisors (supervised); classical FMM planner with PD/line-search velocity generator (not learned)
setting.training_data: Walking policy: RL in RaiSim on procedurally generated fractal terrains with randomized dynamics (friction, payload, etc.). Safety advisors: self-supervised binary labels (in-collision / falls within 1 s) from online sim rollouts with random invisible obstacles, friction, roughness and payload. No navigation-specific training data; the planner is hand-designed.
setting.observation: Proprioception (joint angles/velocities, IMU roll/pitch, binary foot contacts) + egocentric depth (RealSense D435) + VIO pose from RealSense T265 tracking camera; in simulation a ground-truth top-down occupancy map replaces vision
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands (linear v, yaw rate ω) to the walking policy, which outputs 12 joint position targets at 100 Hz (a discrete forward 0.6 m/s / turn ±0.8 rad/s / stop variant is ablated)
setting.simulator: RaiSim (environments built from Gibson and Matterport3D top-down layouts extracted via habitat-sim)
setting.privileged: In simulation: ground-truth occupancy map (plus sim pose). Real robot: none (onboard depth + T265 VIO pose). Point goal given as coordinates.

numbers_note: All simulation results are on the authors' own RaiSim benchmark (200 Gibson/MP3D layouts x 10 goals, called a 'validation set'), with a GT occupancy map. They are not comparable to Habitat PointNav leaderboards. SPL is printed as a fraction (e.g. 0.79) and converted to 0-100 here. Time includes a 220 s timeout penalty for failures; energy covers successful episodes only. VP-Nav Flat time is inconsistent between Table 4 (80.28) and Table 5 (80.87, identical to the RoughTerrain value). Other real-world results (Fig. 6: 5 trials per task, e.g. 100% vs 80%, 100% vs 0%, 80% vs 60%, 100% vs 80% vs 'Only Vision', with an unlabeled second column) appear only in a figure with garbled labels, so they are omitted.
results: On the custom RaiSim point-goal benchmark, the proprioceptive collision detector improves SR over a vision-only coupling by 5.7 points (74.15 vs 68.45, 2 invisible obstacles), rising to 14.9 points with 8 (39.25 vs 24.35). The fall predictor adds about 7 SR points under randomized slippery/rough terrain with payload changes (87.40 vs 80.25). On rough terrain the legged system keeps 95.05 SR / 80.87 s, versus a LoCoBot wheeled baseline at 15.70 (proceed) and 69.10 (avoid, even with GT patch locations). The continuous planner is about 27% faster than a discrete one (80.87 s vs 110.27 s). The emergent-gait policy uses less energy than trot-only (233.05 vs 252.56). On a real Unitree A1 it passes a glass wall 8/8 times, while the vision-only baseline fails every time.
limitations: Simulation experiments assume a ground-truth occupancy map, so the vision part of the system is not evaluated in sim. The benchmark is custom (RaiSim, 200 layouts) and not comparable to standard Habitat PointNav.

The collision detector is purely reactive: it detects unseen obstacles only after physical contact and inserts a fixed-size patch. The fall predictor only adjusts speed and does not reroute around hazardous terrain.
Real-world evaluation is small (5-8 trials per scenario). The planner and thresholds (FMM cost weights, PD gains, velocity increments) are hand-tuned, and FMM local minima can trap the robot.
compares_to: Vision-only VP-Nav without proprioceptive feedback (w/o Proprio)
